cause: NOTE: On April 1, 2021, Mitsubishi Chemical America, Inc. ("MCA") merged its 100 percent owned affiliate Lucite International, Inc. into MCA. Thus, Lucite no longer exists as an entity, and the site was renamed the MCA Beaumont Site. Cause of Event or Excess Opacity Event, or Reason for Scheduled Activity Beginning at approximately 6 AM on the morning of March 29, 2021, the SAR plant began the process of moving from single train to dual train operation by bringing its south furnace online. Bringing the second train online was necessary to reduce the level in the North Spent Acid tank, which contained about 86% capacity at the time. Convertor temperatures were raised in anticipation of bringing the cooler spent acid from the tank instead of the warmer spent acid from the MMA production unit that was being fed to the North furnace. MMA production was maintained at half rates in the dual train configuration to utilize the North tanks acid by about 50 gallons per minute. This procedure drops the spent tank level by about 1.5% per hour. When burning cooler spent acid in the process, the control room operators monitor the convertor temperature. Cooler acid can cause a loss in convertor efficiency, which can allow more SO2 to slip through the convertor and not be converted to SO3. An SO2 slip will go to the SAR main stack and can lead to higher than normal SO2 emissions. When this occurs, the DCS and analyzer systems will detect the higher than normal emissions of SO2 in the SAR stack, which alerts the control room operator that the pound per hour SO2 limit is approaching or surpassed. This high-level alarm occurs when our instantaneous stack emission exceeds 121.67 lb/hr of SO2 (our permitted emission rate). The alarm also activates a rolling 24-hour counter that measures any excess SO2 on an hourly basis, and keeps a running totalized quantity of Total SO2 above permitted limits in order to determine if we are approaching the reportable quantity limit (500 lb. for SO2) in a rolling 24-hour period. On March 29, 2021, our DCS system did not record any hourly emissions of SO2 in excess of the 121.67 lb/hr SO2 limit, leading our control room operations personnel to believe the system was operating within normal parameters. On the afternoon of March 29, a production engineer reviewed operating parameters for the SAR unit. The readings and operating conditions did not seem to support the low emission rates being recorded in the DCS. The engineer informed management of his concerns regarding the readings and parameters, and the decision was made to take the second train off-line as a precautionary measure. The second train was taken off-line beginning at midnight on the 29th and was completely down by 2:00 am on the 30th, after sufficient resources were mobilized to the plant to conduct the necessary controlled shutdown procedures in a safe manner. On the morning of March 30th, a preliminary emission event notification was made as a precautionary measure. On April 1, 2021, MCA began evaluating the SAR & MMA DCS system to determine if a potential permit exceedance occurred or if the original documented emission data was correct. In its preliminary review, MCA identified a calculation methodology error that would affect the DCS calculated emission values imbedded in the DCS system. At this time, it appears that there was an RQ exceedance of 1428.6 pounds of SO2 on March 29 & 30. More information will be available uponcompletion of MCA's review.
actions: As detailed in the event cause, at the time the second train was put on-line, there was no indicated emission exceedance. The site ceased operations on the second train when operating parameters were found to be potentially problematic. By going to single train operation, any excess emissions were ceased. All Sulfuric Acid recovery operations were permanently suspended on April 10, 2021. The plant is being de-inventoried, cleared and cleaned and is scheduled for demolition beginning around July 1, 2021.
basis: The DCS uses six calculations from dozens of operating parameters and continuous emission monitors to calculate the pounds per hour for SO2. The emission rate in lb/hr was determined by multiplying the emissions in lb SO2 /ton of sulfuric acid by the calculated tons of acid produced per day (divided by 24 to units consistent in hours). The tons of acid produced per day is calculated by summing the spent acid and the 98 % acid fed to the system. The highest hourly SO2 hourly emission rate was 116 pounds per hour according to the DCS during the event, which was below the 121.67 pounds per hour allowable. During the audit review, it was determined on April 2, 2021 that a calculated value did not appropriately record the 98% acid feed to the system, which led to an error in the DCS calculating the amount of spent acid produced and, ultimately, the lb/hr of SO2. Once the DCS data was corrected with the new calculation, it was determined that the permit allowable was exceeded for 19 hours from 0700 on March 29, 2021 to 0200 on March 30, 2021. These calculations and data recording systems are still being reviewed with a full report pending. cause: The investigation into the cause for the event on June 12,2021 determined that at 4:04 AM the MTS Liquid Level Control float stuck on the C Decanter (9F404C) in the Natsyn Unit. This caused the level control valve, 9LC404C, to open to 100% and lower the level of the C Decanter. The liquid level readout reported a continual false reading. The C Decanter Water/ No Water Valve, 9LC407C, remained 100% open due to a faulty capacitance probe. The capacitance probe closes the Decanter Water/No Water Valve when hydrocarbons are detected. This caused a discharge of water/hydrocarbon mix into the wastewater trench. The root causes of the event were the stuck float on the MTS Liquid Level Control that indicate a false liquid level in the decanter, and the failure of the capacitance probe to detect the hydrocarbon being discharged from the decanter and close the C Decanter Water/ No Water Valve.
actions: The Board operator identified the C Decanter Water Control Valve (9LC404C) as 100% open. Operator attempted to manipulate the valve to change the water level with no success. The Team Leader went outside to investigate the cause. He tapped on the transmitter, that freed the MTS float and the Water Level Control readout went from 46.3% to 1.7% which automatically closed the C Decanter Water Control Valve (9LC404C). Corrective actions for the failed instruments will be to (1) evaluate another option for a fail-safe instead of a capacitance probe and (2) schedule more frequent periodic maintenance of the MTS probe.
basis: The amount hydrocarbons lost were determined and representative samples were analyzed using a Gas Chromatography Mass Spectrometry to determine the concentration of VOCs released during this event. An estimated total of 10,789.59 lb. of VOCs were released to the atmosphere during this event.

cause: The event was caused by a loss of power from the Entergy Corporation Cheek Substation, which feeds electricity to the Goodyear Beaumont Chemical Plant. After an Entergy technician implemented changes at the substation, both transmission line breakers, 3480 and 3485, tripped at the same time. This caused the entire Goodyear Beaumont Plant to lose electricity.
actions: All operating units followed emergency shutdown procedures designed to minimize emissions. As soon as electricity was restored (10:15 AM), the 3B-106 Steam Boiler was brought online to provide steam assist to the flares to stop the flares from smoking while the units were restarting. Method 22 observations were taken for all three flares. Flare smoking ended at 12:04 PM. During an electric outage, the high- and low-pressure fuel gas (Natural gas) vents valves are designed to open for safety reasons. Once electricity has been restored, the vent valves are designed to close. Electricity to the plant was restored at approximately 10:15 AM. At 10:30 it was discovered that the high-pressure fuel valve failed and did not open, thus did not resume fuel gas flow to the 850 Flare pilot light. Due to the lack of fuel gas flow, the flare pilot was extinguished at 12:30. Goodyear determined that the actuator controlling the high-pressure vent valve had failed as a result of the power outage. The fuel gas remained blocked in for safety purposes. Another actuator control was installed at 14:15 and the fuel gas to the 850 Flare pilot light was relighted at 14:20. During the outage, the Pressure Relieve Valve (PRV) 8F517 to column 8D501 lifted due to over pressurization caused by the electricity outage. This issue was discovered at 19:00 when an operator identified dripping from the PRV. The 8D501 Column was immediately de-inventoried and blocked in and the dripping ceased at 20:20. Goodyear determined that the PRV lifted at 09:17:10 to 09:21:29, but no alarm sounded because of the outage. The dripping was due to the PRV not seating completely and the cooling of the column. The PRV was removed and repaired.
basis: The basis to determine the flare emissions quantities were based off material balance from flare flow rate and the ratio of fuel gas to ratio column flow rates and using the Ideal Gas Law calculations. Emission calculations from the PRV were calculated assuming the PRV lifted between 0-36.5% open for the duration of the over pressurization event using an area estimation of the PRV at the actual temperature and pressure and using the Ideal Gas Law. Emission of the reseat failure used the same calculation method and assuming 0.021% open.

cause: On May 11, 2022 at approximately 23:15 hours, OCI Beaumont Site (OCIB) experienced an interruption in power supply from Electrical Control Room (ECR) 3, which caused the Ammonia Refrigeration train to trip at approximately 23:35 hours and resulted in emissions from Emissions Point (EPN) 45 - Methanol Plant Flare. Emissions from EPN 45 lasted approximately 8 hours with no quantities above the reportable threshold. The interruption of power supply from ECR 3 also resulted in a loss of power to the Pressure Swing Adsorber (PSA) Wash Water pumps. Subsequently, the level in the PSA Wash Water Tower could not be controlled which presented a safety risk for PSA feedgas to breakthrough to the atmospheric crude tank. The PSA was shutdown to mitigate this safety risk at approximately 23:30 hours, which resulted in a sudden reduction in purge feed to the PSA and an increase in pressure in the methanol synthesis loop. Two of three pressure control valves did not respond fast enough to maintain pressure, which resulted in two relief valves lifting per design on the methanol syngas compressor discharge at approximately 23:38 and 23:53 hours, respectively. Emissions were discharged to atmosphere from the relieve valves.
actions: Operations personnel took immediate action to minimize emissions by isolating the relief valves and brought the unit into a safe state. OCIB determined the interruption in power supply was caused by a phase-to-phase electrical fault within the motor starter between the fuses and the contactor. This specific "bucket" is an older design where insulated conductors are in contact between the fuses and the motor contactor. The starter was rebuilt, new fuses installed and insulation on the new wires was reinforced with higher rated tubing to prevent recurrence. OCIB is evaluating options to mitigate any further issues with pressure control on the methanol synthesis loop to prevent recurrence.
basis: Process data and engineer calculations.

cause: On September 09, 2022, INVISTA experienced a sudden and unexpected drop in boiler feed water pressure which caused the North and South Boilers to interlock as designed to protect the boiler. This interlock included an Automatic Waste Feed Cutoff (AWFCO) that is a designed safety feature. Waste gases that were being combusted in the boilers were diverted to the ADN Operating Flare when the boilers interlocked. The high flows and previously undiscovered restrictions in the waste gas flame arrestors upstream of the operating flare resulted in a backpressure increase that caused the backpressure valves to open and vent to the startup flares per design. While attempting to reestablish waste gas flows to the boilers, issues with the waste gas control valves were discovered. Based on the preliminary investigation, INVISTA believes the boilers interlocked due to a sudden drop in Boiler Feed Water header pressure from INVISTA's utility supplier (DOW) lowering the steam drum level while INVISTA's primary Boiler Feed Water Pumps were down for maintenance. The investigation into the loss of feedwater is ongoing.
actions: Immediately upon loss of feedwater pressure, converter rates were reduced to minimum rates and communications to INVISTA's utility supplier were made in attempt to restore Boiler Feed Water header pressure. However, the boilers interlocked prior to re-establishment of the BFW pressure. Once pressure was re-established, the boilers were restarted. Waste gases were reintroduced after the control valve issues were resolved.
basis: The investigation is ongoing, and emissions are based on conservative assumptions and process data calculations from the discovery of the event until response activities were complete.

cause: Due to the severe weather from Winter Storm Elliott, the Boiler 5 steam drum level transmitter experienced a false high level resulting in a shutdown of Boiler 5 at 0:31 hours and again at 9:35 hours. Another shutdown occurred at 18:16 hours due to a loss of boiler feedwater from the third-party supplier's loss of pumps. During these times, Boiler 7 was already down due to the effects of Winter Storm Elliot, which caused a failure of the Boiler 7 main gas valve. With both primary control devices (Boilers 5 and 7) down, the High Pressure Absorber (HPA) overpressured and vented through a relief device which was routed and abated to a control device (No. 1 Vent Stack, EPN PE-20). Low Pressure Diamine Offgas (LPDOG) vented to atmosphere intermittently from the LPDOG header (EPN PE-52) and the D1 and D2 Crude HMD Storage Tanks' Blower RV (EPN PE-55). Emissions from Boiler Stack #3 (Boiler 5 EPN 11 BLR-003) occurred due to re-establishing LPDOG flow during the startup of Boiler 5 in an attempt to minimize uncontrolled emissions to atmosphere. In addition, at the VOC absorber the scrubbing liquid flow was lost due to freezing during the severe weather, reducing the scrubbing efficiency, and resulting in excess emissions to atmosphere (EPN PT60). INVISTA assessed the state of compliance throughout the entirety of the event. During finalization of the emission calculations for the event, it was determined that the emissions were higher than originally estimated and an RQ for ammonia and pentenenitrile was exceeded.
actions: At Boiler 5, INVISTA added extra insulation to the steam drum level transmitter ahead of Winter Storm Elliott; however, the severe winds blew the insulation off. INVISTA immediately began working to re-establish the boiler, and restored the insulation following the first boiler shutdown. With the insulation in place, the freezing cold caused a false high level for the 2nd shutdown. Following the third shutdown of Boiler 5, once the third-party supplier resumed delivery of boiler feedwater, INVISTA re-established fuels to the boiler which stopped the venting. At the VOC absorber, INVISTA began efforts to thaw the line with steam applied externally on 12/23/22 5:00 am; however, due to the ambient temperatures remaining below freezing, and the length of the line, INVISTA was only able to restore flow after ambient temperatures returned to above freezing on 12/24/22 13:00. Once scrubbing liquid flow was restored, the scrubbing efficiency was re-established, and ended the excess emissions.
basis: Process knowledge and engineering calculations were used for determining quantities during this event.

cause: Nitrogen is delivered to the refinery on a pipeline that is owned and operated by a third party. On the pipeline entering the facility, the refinery-owned pressure regulator failed due to metal shavings that originated upstream and outside of the refinery. These shavings were produced during a hot tap connection performed by the third-party nitrogen supply company earlier that day. The failure of the pressure regulator caused a sudden drop in the nitrogen header pressure throughout the refinery. At the Delayed Coking Unit (DCU-844), the Wet Gas Compressor (C-151) tripped due to a low seal pressure differential, which was caused by the low nitrogen supply pressure into the refinery. This resulted in the wet gas header pressuring up and venting to the flare header and reportable sulfur dioxide (SO2) and hydrogen sulfide (H2S) emissions from Flare 26.
actions: Operations opened the bypass around the pressure regulator to increase the refinery's nitrogen header pressure. After stabilizing the Wet Gas Compressor seal pressures, Operations restarted C-151. The wet gas header pressure dropped, and the flaring stopped.
basis: Flow meters, analyzers, and CEMS.

cause: The emissions event occurred on the morning of 2/19/2025 due to a failure to initiate the scrubber system prior to running a reaction in Reactor 14. The emission event ended when the reaction operation was completed, an estimated two hours and eighteen minutes after the start of the reaction. The event was not discovered until 02/21/2025, at which time it was reported promptly. Though the scrubber was not running during the reaction, the emissions did pass through the scrubber / emissions control device, SCRUB1EMUL (Emulsions Scrubber). The ensuing investigation found the primary cause to be that the operator controlling the process failed to start the scrubber prior to the start of the reaction. The Standard Operating Procedure for the activity specified that the scrubber should be running during the operation.
actions: Upon discovery of the emissions event, operation of the associated equipment was stopped. Reporting to STEERS was performed. Reporting requirements per CERCLA and EPCRA regulations were followed. An investigation was performed. The Veolia WTS discipline policy has been enforced to correct the failure to follow the standard operating procedure. The incident has been shared widely across the facility to emphasize the importance of ensuring emissions control devices are operated according to procedure.
basis: When determining the amount of the suspected release involving a chemical reaction, there are various competing reactions (some of which are harmless). The worst case scenario was assumed when calculating the Estimated Quantity released in this report. The Estimated Quantity released is based on analysis of the chemical reaction, material quantities, assays, equipment specifications, and duration of operation.

cause: A malfunction occurred in the facility's boiler system, resulting in a loss of steam production. As a result, the site was unable to supply sufficient steam to the steam-assisted flare. The lack of steam support resulted in elevated opacity levels from the flare, exceeding the 5-minute limit. The Flare BTU remained in compliance, and the flare stayed lit throughout the event, with the flame maintaining a steady orange hue. The issue was promptly investigated, and immediate corrective actions helped eliminate excess opacity.
actions: Upon identifying the boiler malfunction, immediate troubleshooting efforts were made to restore boiler operation; however, these attempts were unsuccessful. To mitigate excess opacity, plant personnel reduced the load on the flare, and production rates on associated process columns were reduced. When the steam supply could not be restored promptly, plant personnel immediately worked on safely shutting down two columns, which stopped the excess opacity. Personnel then worked continuously to repair the boiler, and steam service was successfully restored once the necessary repairs were completed.
basis: Process knowledge. The boiler malfunction was sudden and outside of Monument Chemical Port Arthur's control, marking the first incident in the last three years. As the plant personnel took immediate action to minimize opacity and to stop excess opacity quickly by shutting down two columns, there was no adverse impact on the environment or human health.
